subject: maths
title: Number Bonds to 20 and 100
seo_title: Year 2 Number Bonds Worksheets: Bonds to 10, 20 and 100, Fact Families and Missing Numbers
standard_text: Recall and use addition and subtraction facts to 20 fluently, and derive and use related facts up to 100; show that addition of two numbers can be done in any order (commutative) and subtraction of one number from another cannot; recognise and use the inverse relationship between addition and subtraction and use this to check calculations and solve missing number problems.
meta_desc: Free Year 2 maths worksheets on number bonds: bonds to 10 and 20 with ten frames, fact families, bonds of tens to 100, adding in any order, missing numbers using the inverse, and word problems. 100 questions with an answer key, matched to the National Curriculum.
key_big: Know your bonds to 10, and you can make 20 and 100.
key_sub: 3 + 7 = 10, so 13 + 7 = 20 and 30 + 70 = 100. If 8 + 5 = 13, then 13 − 5 = 8. You can add in any order, but you cannot swap the numbers in a subtraction.
body_html:
What is a number bond?

A number bond is a pair of numbers that make a total. 7 and 3 make 10, so 7 + 3 = 10 is a number bond to 10. Learn the bonds to 10 by heart. Then you can use them to make 20 and 100.

Bonds to 10Bonds to 20Bonds to 100
1 + 911 + 910 + 90
2 + 812 + 820 + 80
3 + 713 + 730 + 70
4 + 614 + 640 + 60
5 + 515 + 550 + 50

From 10 to 20 and 100

13 is 10 and 3. You know 3 + 7 = 10. So 13 + 7 = 20. In the same way, 3 tens + 7 tens = 10 tens, so 30 + 70 = 100.

Example

Find the missing number: 60 + ? = 100

6 + 4 = 10, so 6 tens + 4 tens = 10 tens = 100.

Answer: 40

Fact families

A part-whole model shows two parts and the whole. One model gives four facts. If you know 8 + 5 = 13, you also know 13 − 5 = 8.

Does the order matter?

You can add in any order: 6 + 9 = 9 + 6. You cannot swap the numbers in a subtraction: 9 − 6 = 3, but 6 − 9 is not 3.

Check with the inverse

Addition and subtraction undo each other. To check 15 − 7 = 8, add: 8 + 7 = 15. Use the same idea for missing numbers.

Example

Find the missing number: ? − 6 = 9

Add back the 6: 9 + 6 = 15. Check: 15 − 6 = 9.

Answer: 15

Common mistakes

MistakeWhat to do instead
Bonds to 10 out by one: 6 + 5 = 10Use a ten frame: 6 counters and 4 spaces, so 6 + 4 = 10
13 + ? = 20 gives 1713 is 10 and 3. 3 + 7 = 10, so 13 + 7 = 20
30 + 70 = 10 or 1,0003 tens + 7 tens = 10 tens, and 10 tens = 100
13 − 5 = 18, or 7Think: 5 + 8 = 13, so 13 − 5 = 8
Swapping a subtraction: 9 − 6 = 6 − 9Only addition can be done in any order

faq.q: What are number bonds in Year 2?
faq.a: Number bonds are pairs of numbers that make a total, like 7 + 3 = 10 or 13 + 7 = 20. In Year 2, children use bonds to 10 to find bonds to 20 and bonds of tens to 100, such as 30 + 70 = 100.

faq.q: What number bonds should a Year 2 child know?
faq.a: By the end of Year 2, the National Curriculum expects children to recall addition and subtraction facts to 20 fluently. They should also use them to work out related facts up to 100, like 40 + 60 = 100 and 100 − 40 = 60.
A fact family is the set of four facts made from the same three numbers. For 8, 5 and 13 they are 8 + 5 = 13, 5 + 8 = 13, 13 − 5 = 8 and 13 − 8 = 5.

faq.q: How can I help my child learn number bonds at home?
faq.a: Use a ten frame, an egg box or ten fingers to show the pairs that make 10, and practise for a few minutes every day. Once bonds to 10 are quick, ask “if 3 + 7 = 10, what is 13 + 7 or 30 + 70?”

items.e: There are 7 counters and 3 empty spaces. 7 + 3 = 10, so 3 more fill the frame.

items.e: There are 4 counters and 6 empty spaces. 4 + 6 = 10, so 6 more fill the frame.

items.e: There are 9 counters and 1 empty space. 9 + 1 = 10, so 1 more fills the frame.

items.q: What is the missing part?
items.e: The parts make the whole. 2 + 8 = 10, so the missing part is 8. (12 adds instead: 10 + 2.)

3 and 7 make 10. So the missing number is 7. Check: 3 + 7 = 10.

How many more counters make 20?
items.e: The top frame is full: 10. The bottom frame has 4, with 6 empty spaces. So 6 more make 20.

items.q: How many more counters make 20?
items.e: The top frame is full: 10. The bottom frame has 7, with 3 empty spaces. So 3 more make 20.

items.q: What is the missing part?
items.e: 15 is 10 and 5. 5 + 5 = 10, and 10 + 10 = 20. So the missing part is 5. Check: 15 + 5 = 20.
13 is 10 and 3. 3 + 7 = 10, and 10 + 10 = 20. So the missing number is 7. Check: 13 + 7 = 20.
16 is 10 and 6. 6 + 4 = 10, and 10 + 10 = 20. So the missing number is 4. Check: 16 + 4 = 20.
12 is 10 and 2. 2 + 8 = 10, and 10 + 10 = 20. So the missing number is 8. Check: 12 + 8 = 20.
11 is 10 and 1. 1 + 9 = 10, and 10 + 10 = 20. So the missing number is 9. Check: 11 + 9 = 20.
5 + 5 = 10. You need 10 more to make 20. 5 + 10 = 15, so the missing number is 15. Check: 5 + 15 = 20.
3 + 7 = 10. You need 10 more to make 20. 7 + 10 = 17, so the missing number is 17. Check: 3 + 17 = 20.

items.q: How many more from 18 make 20?
items.e: Count on from 18: 19, 20. That is 2. 8 + 2 = 10, so 18 + 2 = 20.

items.q: The frames show 8 + 5 = 13. What is 13 − 5?
items.e: Take away the 5 blue counters. The 8 red counters are left. 13 − 5 = 8.
If 8 + 5 = 13, then 13 − 8 = 5. Subtraction undoes addition.

items.q: Which subtraction matches the model?
items.e: Start with the whole and take away one part. The other part is left: 13 − 8 = 5.

items.q: Which addition matches the model?
items.e: Add the two parts to get the whole: 12 + 8 = 20.

items.q: Which fact is in the same family as 7 + 4 = 11?
items.e: A fact family uses the same three numbers: 7, 4 and 11. 11 − 4 = 7 uses them all.

items.q: Which fact is NOT in the fact family for 6, 9 and 15?
items.e: 9 − 6 = 3 uses the number 3, not 15. The others use only 6, 9 and 15.

items.q: How many facts are in the fact family for 5, 8 and 13?

items.e: Think: 5 + 8 = 13. So 13 − 5 = 8. (12 comes from 5 − 3 in the ones.)
Think: 6 + 8 = 14. So 14 − 6 = 8. (12 comes from 6 − 4 in the ones.)
Think: 6 + 14 = 20. So 20 − 6 = 14. (4 is the bond to 10, not to 20.)
Think: 3 + 8 = 11. So 11 − 3 = 8. (12 comes from 3 − 1 in the ones.)
Add the answer to the number you took away. 8 + 8 = 16, so 16 − 8 = 8 is right.

items.q: What is the whole?
items.e: The whole is the two parts added: 6 + 9 = 15. (3 is 9 − 6.)

items.q: What is the missing part?
items.e: Whole − part = the other part. 17 − 9 = 8. Check: 9 + 8 = 17.

items.q: Count on in tens from 70 to 100. How much is that?
items.e: There are 3 jumps of 10. 3 tens = 30. Check: 70 + 30 = 100.
8 tens − 3 tens = 5 tens = 50.
6 tens − 4 tens = 2 tens = 20.

You can add in any order. 9 + 6 is the same as 6 + 9, so the answer is 15.

items.q: Which has the same answer as 7 + 8?
items.e: Addition can be done in any order. 8 + 7 = 15, and 7 + 8 = 15.
Swapping the numbers in an addition gives the same answer: 6 + 9 = 9 + 6. You cannot swap the numbers in a subtraction.
No. 12 − 5 means take 5 from 12. 5 − 12 means take 12 from 5. Order matters in subtraction.

items.q: You can swap the numbers in one of these and get the same answer. Which one?
items.e: Only addition can be done in any order. 4 + 11 = 11 + 4 = 15. So the answer is 4 + 11.

items.q: Ruby says 10 − 3 is the same as 3 − 10. Is she right?
items.e: 10 − 3 = 7, but you cannot take 10 from 3 and get 7. Order matters in subtraction.

items.q: Which two additions match the model?
items.e: The parts are 8 and 6. You can add them in any order: 8 + 6 = 14 and 6 + 8 = 14.
Use the inverse. 9 + 6 = 15. Check: 15 − 6 = 9. (3 is 9 − 6.)
Use the inverse. 15 − 7 = 8. Check: 8 + 7 = 15.
Think: 6 + ? = 14. 6 + 8 = 14, so the missing number is 8.
Use the inverse. 50 + 30 = 80. Check: 80 − 30 = 50.
Use the inverse. 100 − 40 = 60. Check: 60 + 40 = 100.
Think: 9 + ? = 17. 9 + 8 = 17, so the missing number is 8.
Use the inverse. 12 + 8 = 20. Check: 20 − 8 = 12.

items.q: Isla says 13 − 4 = 8. Check with addition. Is she right?
items.e: Add the answer and the number taken away: 8 + 4 = 12, not 13. So she is not right. 13 − 4 = 9.

items.q: Harry says 100 − 60 = 40. Which addition checks it?
items.e: Add the answer to the number taken away: 40 + 60 = 100. So Harry is right.

items.q: A page in Oliver’s football sticker album holds 20 stickers. He has stuck in 13. How many more stickers does he need to fill the page?
Amelia has 15 sweets. She eats 6. How many sweets are left?
items.e: She eats some, so subtract. 15 − 6 = 9. Check: 9 + 6 = 15.

items.q: There are 20 children on a bus. 8 children get off. How many children are still on the bus?
items.e: Children get off, so subtract. 20 − 8 = 12. Check: 12 + 8 = 20.

items.q: There are 12 children on a bus. 8 more get on. How many children are on the bus now?
items.e: More get on, so add. 2 + 8 = 10, so 12 + 8 = 20.

items.q: A box holds 10 eggs. There are 6 eggs in it. How many more eggs will fill the box?
items.e: 6 + 4 = 10. So 4 eggs will fill the box.

items.q: A jigsaw has 100 pieces. Harry has put in 60 pieces. How many pieces are left?
items.e: 6 + 4 = 10, so 60 + 40 = 100. 40 pieces are left.

items.q: Lily has 30p. A comic costs £1. How much more money does she need?
items.e: £1 = 100p. 30 + 70 = 100, so she needs 70p more.

items.q: Grace has run 70 m of a 100 m race. How far is it to the finish?
items.e: 70 + 30 = 100. It is 30 m to the finish.

items.q: There are 20 pupils in a class. 11 are girls. How many are boys?
Arjun has 7 red pencils and 8 blue pencils. How many pencils does he have?
items.e: Put them together, so add. 7 + 8 = 15. (1 is 8 − 7.)

items.q: Freya had some marbles. She gave away 5. Now she has 9. How many marbles did she have at first?
items.e: Use the inverse. Add back the 5 she gave away: 9 + 5 = 14. Check: 14 − 5 = 9.

items.q: Noah scores 6 points and then 9 points. Kai scores 9 points and then 6 points. Who has more points?
items.e: 6 + 9 = 15 and 9 + 6 = 15. You can add in any order, so they have the same.

items.q: A plate has 16 biscuits. The children eat 9. How many biscuits are left?
Ava has 40 beads. She needs 100 beads for a necklace. How many more beads does she need?
items.e: 4 + 6 = 10, so 40 + 60 = 100. She needs 60 beads.

items.q: A car park has 100 spaces. 50 cars are parked. How many spaces are empty?
items.e: 5 + 5 = 10, so 50 + 50 = 100. 50 spaces are empty.

items.q: George counts 14 people on the top deck of a bus. There are 20 seats. How many seats are empty?
items.e: 14 + 6 = 20. So 6 seats are empty.

items.q: Maya has 18 stickers. She gives 9 to her friend. How many stickers does she have now?
Jack has some football cards. He gets 6 more. Now he has 13. How many did he have at first?
items.e: Use the inverse. Take away the 6 new cards: 13 − 6 = 7. Check: 7 + 6 = 13.

items.q: Zara has 80p. She spends 30p on a pencil. How much money does she have left?
items.e: 8 tens − 3 tens = 5 tens. 80p − 30p = 50p.

items.q: Charlie had 20 conkers. He lost some. Now he has 12. How many conkers did he lose?
items.e: 20 − ? = 12. Think: 12 + 8 = 20. He lost 8 conkers.
